{{Short description|Differential equation in a power system}}
{{redirect|Torque angle|machine assembly technique|Torque-angle tension control}}
A [[power system]] consists of a number of [[alternator|synchronous machines]] operating synchronously under all operating conditions. Under normal operating conditions, the relative position of the rotor axis and the resultant [[magnetic field]] axis is fixed. The angle between the two is known as the '''power angle''',  '''torque angle''', or '''rotor angle'''. During any disturbance, the rotor decelerates or accelerates with respect to the synchronously rotating air gap [[magnetomotive force]], creating relative motion. The equation describing the relative motion is known as the swing equation, which is a non-linear second order [[differential equation]] that describes the swing of the rotor of synchronous machine. The power exchange between the mechanical rotor and the [[electrical grid]] due to the rotor swing (acceleration and deceleration) is called [[Inertial response]].

==Derivation==

A [[synchronous generator]] is driven by a prime mover. The equation governing the rotor motion is given by:{{sfn|Grainger|Stevenson|1994|pp=698-702}}
<math display="block">J\frac{d^2{\theta_\text{m}}}{dt^2} = T_a  = T_\text{m} - T_\text{e},</math>
where:

*<math>J</math> is the total [[moment of inertia]] of the rotor mass in kg-m<sup>2</sup>
*<math>\theta_\text{m}</math> is the [[Angular displacement|angular position]] of the rotor with respect to a stationary axis in radians (rad)
*<math>t</math> is time in seconds (s)
*<math>T_a</math> is the net accelerating [[torque]], in '''N'''-m
*<math>T_\text{m}</math> is the mechanical torque supplied by the prime mover in '''N'''-m
*<math>T_\text{e}</math> is the electrical torque output of the alternator in '''N'''-m

Neglecting losses, the difference between the mechanical and electrical torque gives the net accelerating torque <math>T_a</math>. In the steady state, the electrical torque is equal to the mechanical torque and hence the accelerating power is zero. During this period the rotor moves at synchronous speed <math>\omega_s</math> in rad/s. The electric torque <math>T_\text{e}</math> corresponds to the net air-gap power in the machine and thus accounts for the total output power of the generator plus [[Electric power#Resistive circuits|<math>|I|^2 R</math> losses]] in the [[armature (electrical engineering)|armature]] winding.{{sfn|Umans|2013|pp=263-264}}

The angular position <math>\theta</math> is measured with a stationary reference frame. Representing it with respect to the synchronously rotating frame gives:
<math display="block">\theta_\text{m} = \omega_\text{sm}t  + \delta_\text{m},</math>
where the mechanical power angle <math>\delta_m</math> is the angular position with respect to the synchronously rotating reference frame. The derivative of the above equation with respect to time is:
<math display="block">\frac{d\theta_\text{m}}{dt} = \omega_\text{sm} + \frac{d\delta_\text{m}}{dt}.</math>
The above equations show that the rotor angular speed is equal to the synchronous speed only when <math>d\delta_m /dt</math> is equal to zero. Therefore, the term <math>d\delta_m /dt</math> represents the deviation of the rotor speed from synchronism in rad/s.

By taking the second order derivative of the above equation it becomes:
<math display="block">\frac{d^2\theta_\text{m}}{dt^2} = \frac{d^2\delta_\text{m}}{dt^2}.</math>
Substituting the above equation in the equation of rotor motion gives:
<math display="block">J\frac{d^2{\delta_\text{m}}}{dt^2} = T_a = T_\text{m} - T_\text{e}.</math>
Multiplying both sides by the [[angular velocity]] of the rotor, given by 
<math display="block">\omega_\text{m} = \frac{{d\theta_\text{m}}}{dt},</math> 
results in
<math display="block">J\omega_\text{m}\frac{d^2{\delta_\text{m}}}{dt^2} = P_a = P_\text{m} - P_\text{e},</math>
where <math>P_a</math>, <math>P_\text{m}</math> and <math>P_\text{e}</math> respectively are the accelerating, mechanical and electrical ([[AC power#Real power|active]]) power in [[Watt]] (W). Intuitivley, the equation can also be derived by taking the [[time derivative]] of the [[rotational energy]].

The [[coefficient]] <math>J \omega_{\text{m}}</math> is the [[angular momentum]] of the rotor at synchronous speed <math>\omega_{\text{sm}}</math>. In machine data supplied for stability studies this coefficient is often denoted by <math>M</math> and called the ''[[inertia constant]]'' of the machine. In practice, <math>\omega_{\text{m}}</math> does not differ significantly from synchronous speed when the machine is in steady state <math>\omega_{\text{sm}}</math>; allowing for another constant of inertia:{{sfn|Saadat|1999|pp=462-463}}
<math display="block">H = \frac{\frac{1}{2}J\omega_\text{sm}^2}{S_{\text{rated}}}= \frac{\frac{1}{2}M \omega_\text{sm}}{S_{\text{rated}}}= \frac{\text{stored kinetic energy in mega joules at synchronous speed}}{\text{machine rating in MVA}},</math>
where <math>S_{\text{rated}}</math> is the [[Three-phase electric power|three phase]] rating of the machine in [[Volt-ampere|MVA]]. Substituting in the above equation
<math display="block">2H\frac{S_{\text{rated}}}{\omega_\text{sm}^2}\omega_\text{m}\frac{d^2{\delta_\text{m}}}{dt^2} = P_\text{m} - P_\text{e} = P_a.</math>
Since <math>P_\text{m}</math>, <math>P_\text{e}</math> and <math>P_a</math> in the machine data are given in MW, dividing them by the generator MVA rating gives these quantities in per unit. Dividing the above equation on both sides by <math>S_{\text{rated}}</math> gives
{{Equation box 1
|indent = :
|equation = <math>\frac{2H}{\omega_\text{s}}\frac{d^2{\delta}}{dt^2} = P_\text{m} - P_e = P_a </math> per unit
|cellpadding= 5
|border
|border colour = #0073CF
|bgcolor=#F9FFF7
}}
with the electrical power angle and electrical angular velocity given by
<math display="block">\delta = \frac{p}{2}\delta_m, \qquad
\omega = \frac{p}{2}\omega_m, \qquad
\omega_s = \frac{p}{2}\omega_{sm},</math>
where <math>p</math> is the number of poles of the synchronous machine.

The above equation describes the behaviour of the rotor dynamics and hence is known as the '''swing equation'''. The angle <math>\delta</math> is that of the internal [[Electromotive force|EMF]] <math>(E)</math> of the [[synchronous generator]] and dictates the amount of power that can be transferred. This angle is therefore called the '''power angle'''. Neglecting the machine's resistive losses, the corresponding power angle equation is:{{sfn|Grainger|Stevenson|1994|pp=709-712}}
<math display="block">P_e = P_{max} \sin (\delta)=3\frac{|V||E|}{X}\sin (\delta),</math>
where <math>X</math> is the machine [[Inductive reactance|reactance]] and <math>V</math> the system (i.e. grid) voltage.{{sfn|Schavemaker|van der Sluis|2008|pp=71-74}} The angle <math>\delta</math> is also referred to as the '''torque angle''' as the electrical torque <math>T_e</math> can be derived from this equation as{{sfn|Chapman|2011|loc=chpt. 4.6 Power and Torque in Synchronous Generators}} 
<math display="block"> T_e = \frac{P_e}{\omega_m}=3\frac{|V||E|}{\omega_m X}\sin (\delta).</math>
Hence, for synchronous machines the swing equation is a non-linear function of <math>\delta</math> and can be solved numerically using, e.g., the [[Runge–Kutta methods|fourth-order Runge-Kutta algorithm]]. When <math>\delta</math> is small, the equation can be linearized as <math>P_e \approx P_{max}\delta</math>.{{sfn|Guru|Hiziroǧlu|2001|pp=648-651}}
